A black stone is found in the Nile similar to a bean; upon seeing this, dogs do not bark. You may carry a dog’s tongue placed under the great toe in your shoe, or carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to <term>Sextus</term> <note>likely Sextus Placitus, author of a late antique medicinal text on animal remedies</note>. According to <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History</note>, use a hare's fur or dung. Or you may carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give a dog a frog in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. <term>Nigidius</term> <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> says that dogs will flee the sight of anyone for the whole day who removes a tick from a pig and carries it about for a little while. <term>Oppianus</term> <note>Oppian of Apamea, author of a Greek poem on hunting</note> says:

> But if you carry a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Both puppies and fierce dogs will immediately be struck
> With sharp terror, and they shall not bark at you hereafter
> As you walk along, even if they had barked before.

### How to make it so a dog cannot run.

If you smear its wings <note>referring to the hollows of the joints or armpits</note> with oil, it will be hindered in its running; this happens in that manner.

### How to make a hawk courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the meat which it uses during the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from your own beak <note>your mouth</note> into the beak of a young pigeon and then let it fly. Thus:

### You shall make partridges more combative,

If you give them sprigs of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. And:

### Roosters become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food when they are soon to fight. For this reason, in the Old Comedy, they were most wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <note>original: "ἐσκοροδισμένοι"</note>, that is, "fed on garlic," meaning someone who is vehement and far too prone to a fight.

### So that a bird does not fly high,

Pluck out the tail feathers which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly at all,

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing; it remains without further harm, but the bird will not fly. In this manner, they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page details folkloric and natural methods for controlling animals, including preventing dogs from barking or running and using wine or garlic to increase the aggression of hawks and roosters.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting lore, dogs, falconry, roosters, garlic, Pliny, Oppian, folk remedies</keywords>

shines through piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if seen by the eyes through true reason. By the confidence of his belief, he stands out among men as much as the sun excels the other stars by its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this is the second god, O Asclepius, who governs the rest and illuminates all worldly beings, whether they are endowed with souls or are inanimate. For if the world is a living creature <note>the concept of "Anima Mundi" or the World Soul</note> always living, and was, and is, and shall be, nothing in the world is mortal. For since every single part of a living being is in the world itself, as in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. Consequently, just as the world is eternal, so too is the sun itself always the governor of vital things, or rather the cultivator and dispenser of their entire vitality. God, therefore, is the eternal governor of living beings, or of the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. Once, however, he dispensed life to all vital beings by an eternal law, in this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains to Asclepius that the pious man excels others like the sun among stars. He describes the world as an eternally living being governed by the sun, asserting that within this divine system, true mortality does not exist.</summary>

<keywords>piety, religion, sun, Asclepius, World Soul, eternity, governor of life, immortality, divine law</keywords>

And there are wonders even greater than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lute. At Megara, a certain rock plays like a lyre when struck by pebbles, so great is the power of Music. It <note>Music</note> softens the soul, lifts the mind, incites warriors to war, and eases the labor and fatigue of every individual task. It recalls those who have fallen or are in despair, and strengthens travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are strengthened by their singing drivers. In a similar way, those carrying heavy loads sing, and are made more capable and lightened by it: for song produces delight and ability; it mitigates the wrathful, cheers the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, tempers the madness of the frantic, and dissipates vain thoughts. Hence it is that <term>Democritus</term> and <term>Theophrastus</term> affirm that certain diseases of the body and mind can be either cured or induced in this way. You have understood, my son, the manner of **rebirth** <note>original: "regenerationis"</note> itself. Since the **number ten** <note>original: "denario numero"</note> is present, the intellectual generation is completed, which rejects the **number twelve** <note>original: "duodenarium numerum"</note>. We have observed this from the generation itself. Therefore, whoever loses their physical senses because of the goodness of that generation which is according to God, knows themselves to be composed of divine things. Having become steadfast, they rejoice with their whole mind in divine power.

**TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the sight of my eyes, but by the action of the mind, which is exercised through inner powers. I am in heaven; I am in the earth, in the water, in the air. I am in the animals, in the trees; I am in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I wish you would tell me further: how are the avenging darknesses, twelve in number, repelled by the ten powers? By what means, Trismegistus?

**HERMES.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the **circle of the zodiac** <note>original: "ex zodiaco circulo"</note>, which consists of that number twelve. The numbers are eleven; one is of all forms according to the ideas of nature, regarding the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avenging forces are in a certain way separated from one another, yet in their action they are in some way joined; as you see, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly then, according to correct reason, there is an interval insofar as they are repelled by the ten **effective powers** <note>original: "apotellatibus"; likely a corruption or variant of "apotelesmatibus," referring to the divine influences or results</note>, that is, by the number ten. For the number ten, O son, is the parent of the soul, while Life and 

<summary>Hermes explains how the ten divine powers of the decade overcome the twelve zodiacal vices of the body, allowing Tatius to experience a mystical omnipresence beyond the physical senses.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Tatius, rebirth, regeneration, decade, number ten, zodiac, number twelve, omnipresence, intellectual generation</keywords>

These are followed by the gods whose chief is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence or being</gloss>. These are the sensible gods, similar to their dual origin, who produce all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work through the other. Jupiter is the <term>ousiarch</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> of heaven, or whatever is understood by that name; for through heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. The <term>ousiarch</term> of the sun is light, for the good of light is poured into us through the orb of the sun. There are thirty-six <note>referring to the decans of the zodiac</note>, whose name is "Horoscopes," fixed forever in the same place as the stars. Their <term>ousiarch</term> or prince is the one they call <term>Pantomorphos</term> <gloss>All-formed</gloss>, who creates diverse forms from diverse species. The seven spheres, which are called the wanderers <note>the planets</note>, have their own <term>ousiarchs</term>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune or <term>Heimarmene</term> <gloss>Fate</gloss>. By these, all things are changed by the law of nature with the firmest stability, and varied by eternal agitation. The air, however, is the instrument or the engine of all, through which all things are made. There is also a second <term>ousiarch</term> of this <note>referring to the air or lower realm</note>, who governs mortals and things similar to them. Since these things are arranged this way, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are so naturally connected that mortals are bound to mortals and sensible things to sensible things. Yet the height of the governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, but rather one. For since all things hang from one, and rather flow from Him, when they are seen at a distance, they are believed to be many and separate. In truth, however, they are joined as one, or rather two: that from which all things are made and He by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they consist and by the will of Him by whose nod other things are brought to pass. ASCLEPIUS: What is this reasoning again, O Trismegistus? TRISMEGISTUS: It is such, O Asclepius. For God, or the Father, or the Lord...

<summary>Trismegistus explains the hierarchy of divine rulers or ousiarchs who govern heaven, the sun, the zodiacal decans, and the planets. He emphasizes that despite the appearance of multiplicity, all creation remains a unified whole depending on a single source and divine will.</summary>
<keywords>Ousia, Ousiarch, Jupiter, Sun, Light, Pantomorphos, Fate, Heimarmene, Planetary Spheres, Unity of Being, Asclepius</keywords>

showed itself. For indeed, arsenic can by no means be fixed unless the operator is an artist who understands its tinting spirit in equal measure. In this matter, all philosophers have slumbered, laboring in vain to produce anything from it. Therefore, whoever remains ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the power by which the perfection of transmutation is acquired. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention was made is drawn from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened but not changed. The Sophists mixed Venus <note>copper</note> disguised and painted in this manner with twice its weight of Luna <note>silver</note>, and sold it to goldsmiths and coin-makers. Eventually, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters—not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the Sophists took red arsenic instead of white, and this itself resulted in a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it exhibits nothing beyond whiteness.

Some proceeded further to common sulfur, which they cooked until yellow with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urine, day and night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they raised it from common salt and the lime of eggshells by sublimation. They cooked and sublimated it many times, yet it remained combustible nonetheless, even though it was white. However, they believed they could fix raw mercury with it.

<summary>Paracelsus warns that chemical whitening of copper with arsenic is a superficial deception used by counterfeiters and explains why common sulfur remains combustible despite repeated purification.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, fixation, copper, silver, counterfeiters, sulfur, sublimation, mercury, alchemy, sophists</keywords>

Our matter, however, is bought from no shop, yet it is found daily in such places, and merchants cast it out into the streets. It is enough that it be found for free: But the matter of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>lapis</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor. For our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>ærugo</gloss>, <term>saltpeter</term> <gloss>halonitrum</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <gloss>salmiacum</gloss>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite others of that kind. Yet it is not dug out from wild and rustic mountains with hammers and other instruments: But our stone is drawn only from our mountains and springs; our <term>Salt</term> is found in our <term>Salt-spring</term>; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are poured out, and not from wild, foreign, and rustic mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all of this, nor can they believe or comprehend it; for the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses. For this reason they have used these things otherwise than was proper, and have by no means aimed at the mark. Nevertheless, they have persisted in that contrary sense and yielded to their own stubborn heads; just as when they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimated</term> <gloss>converted to vapor</gloss> with a strong fire, scorched with <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>corrosive acids</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, when they ought to have <term>dissolved</term> <gloss>solvere</gloss>, they <term>congealed</term> <gloss>coagularunt</gloss> there, and again, like men unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and repeatedly claimed with lying words that the art was not true, but false, in which point they themselves are deservedly lying: for their own ignorance has shamefully deceived them. This must be attributed to their own obscure and murky cleverness, while, according to their own dark understanding, they interpreted words differently than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), then those unskilled <term>little philosophers</term> <gloss>Philosophastri</gloss> understood it to mean burning, and they reduced things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Also, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, then those <term>would-be-wise</term> <gloss>nasutuli</gloss> burned nature with <term>strong water</term>, and with that same water, which has no...

This allows a greater fire to be applied to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err regarding <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction <note>the process of returning a metal from its lime to its metallic state</note>. For if he attempts the reduction of its lime, it may happen that it does not reduce, but remains in its prior state or is converted into glass, leading him to think its reduction is impossible. We say that if a great fire is not applied in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term> <margin>cc</margin>, it will not reduce. Yet even with a great fire, it does not necessarily reduce, but it is possible for it to turn into glass. This is because <term>Jupiter</term> <margin>am</margin> <margin>ta</margin> <margin>cc</margin> contains within the depth of its nature a fugitive substance of <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver or mercury</gloss>. If this remains too long in the fire, it will flee, leaving the body deprived of its moisture. Thus, it is found to be more fit for vitrification <note>turning into glass</note> than for the fusion of a metallic body <margin>cc</margin>. For everything deprived of its own moisture provides no fusion except that which leads to glass <margin>cc</margin>. Therefore, it is necessary to hasten the reduction quickly with a very swift force of fire. Otherwise, it is not reduced. Let the practitioner be trained in this, and he shall know.

The <gloss>second</gloss> method of calcination for these <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss> two bodies, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt <margin>85, 6</margin>, is as follows: a quantity of salt should be thrown upon their surface, bit by bit, very often during their fusion. They should be mixed with much stirring by an iron <margin>wood. it boils. See page 57, 14.</margin> rod over the fire, until they are turned into ash through the mixing of the salt. Afterward, the lime of these metals is perfected by the same method of perfection, following the proper considerations. But there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. For <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> is converted into powder more easily during the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> has a more fixed moisture than <term>Jupiter</term>.

829. Since Religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from these highest parts the lower things live and shine, and because **Mohammed** <note>original: "Mahumedes"</note> is present in their minds together with their religion, there is always some Mohammed placed in their sight. So that they may turn their faces toward the East, over which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian Center <note>original: "Meditullium Christianum"</note>. This is not the Mohammed himself who wrote the **Koran** <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same person, but he is changed. Once there was one from **Saxony** who, having been captured by **Algerians** and made a Mohammedan, had also been a Christian; he was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the Son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Other Mohammeds succeeded this one afterward. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like torches so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to any others but the Mohammedans.

830. The real Mohammed who wrote the Koran does not come into sight today. I was told that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as a God, he was cast out from his seat, which he held under the Papists, and was sent down to the right side near the south. Once a certain society of Mohammedans was incited by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God; to settle the sedition, Mohammed was raised up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared similar to corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face verging toward black; and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink down.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and the resulting worship of three Gods and as many Creators; and toward the Roman Catholics additionally because of their kneeling before images. For this reason, they call the latter Idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," thus splitting the Omnipotence and making three out of the one and only. They say Christians are like **Fauns** <note>mythological creatures, often depicted as wild or deceptive</note> with three horns, one for each God, and yet three for one; and that they thus pray, thus sing, and thus sound from their pulpits.

832. Like all nations who acknowledge one God, love what is just, and do good from a religious motive, the Mohammedans have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two: in the lower one they live honorably with several wives, but from there none are raised into the higher Heaven except those who give up their concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the faith among them by which an ascent into the higher Heaven is given to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion may be a stumbling block to those who think about **Divine Providence** and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except one born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a stumbling block to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these people inquire into its purpose and they find it. It is in this: that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God; but because they have made only the Koran the book of their religion, and thus Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled in their thoughts and they follow him with some worship, they think little about our Lord. In order that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up from the Lord's Divine Providence to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be described in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. ### On the images of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon. Cap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon <note>referring to the lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>, namely the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter with the head <note>the North Node</note> held the midheaven. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions, and they intended to denote by that image a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit or guiding intelligence</gloss>. They wished to represent him by the image of a serpent: for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all other animals, and praise its divine nature: because within it, more than in other animals, there exists a sharper spirit and a greater fire. This quality is shown by its swift movement without any feet or hands or other instruments, and also because it repeatedly renews its age with its cast-off skin and becomes young again. From this, he concluded that the world was created through <term>Will</term> <gloss>al-irāda</gloss>. 

The premise stating that the Will is what specifies one of two identical possibilities is correct. However, the premise stating that the world is situated in an encompassing void is either false or not self-evident. Furthermore, his assumption of this void leads to a conclusion they <note>the theologians</note> find abominable: that the void would be eternal. This is because if the void were created, it would itself require another void in which to exist.

As for the premise stating that the Will can only produce a created <note>temporal</note> object, that is not self-evident. This is because the "Will in act" <note>will that is currently being exercised</note> exists alongside the "willed act" itself. Will is a relative term <note>original: *min al-muḍāf*</note>, and it has been demonstrated that when one of two relative terms exists in act, the other must also exist in act, such as father and son. Similarly, if one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. Therefore, if the Will in act is created, the willed object must necessarily be created in act. If the Will in act is eternal, then the willed object in act is eternal.

As for the will that precedes the willed object, that is "Will in potentiality." This refers to a will whose object has not yet emerged into actuality, because the action required for the occurrence of the willed object has not yet been joined to that will. It is clear that when its willed object emerges, the Will enters a state of existence it was not in before the object became actual, as the Will is the cause of the object’s occurrence through the medium of action. Thus, if the <term>Mutakallimun</term> <gloss>theologians of Kalam</gloss> were to posit that the Will is created, it would necessarily follow that the willed object is created.

The apparent meaning of the <term>Sharia</term> <gloss>divine law/revelation</gloss> is that it does not enter into such deep technicalities with the common people. For this reason, it does not explicitly state whether the Will is eternal or created. Instead, it states what is most apparent: that the Will brings created beings into existence. This is found in the words of the Exalted: "Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is but that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is" <note>Quran 16:40</note>. This was phrased this way because the common people do not understand how created things can come from an eternal Will. In truth, the <term>Sharia</term> did not specify whether the Will is created or eternal because this is among the <unclear>difficult matters of philosophy</unclear>...

But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we—as citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—venerate and love through the holy celestial angels and the powers of God, who are most blessed: He forbids sacrifice [to others], thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people. And he brought it in quite threateningly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone should think that the command was not to sacrifice to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits—whom this man [Porphyry] calls the "least" or "lesser" ones—who even in the Holy Scriptures are themselves called gods, not of the Hebrews

but of the Gentiles: this is clearly stated in the Psalm where the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint: the Greek translation of the Old Testament produced by seventy scholars</note> wrote, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Therefore, lest anyone think it was prohibited to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to all or some of the celestial beings, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only; lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" should believe there is anyone else besides the God to whom he thinks sacrifice must be made. That it should be understood in this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews—to whom even this great philosopher offers such grand testimony—gave the Law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; it is not obscure or unknown, but is already famous among all nations. In this Law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to search for many things in his Law and his prophets concerning this matter? Indeed, do not search for them: for they are not obscured or erased, but are clear and frequent to gather. I place them in this disputation of mine because they appear clearer than light: that the true and supreme God willed that sacrifice be made to none at all except only to himself. Behold this one thing, stated briefly yet grandly, threateningly but truly, by that God whom the most learned of those men preach as so excellent: let them hear it, let them fear it, let them fulfill it, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follow. "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," he says, "except to the Lord only." Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we belong to him. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, You are my God, for you do not need my goods." Of this God, we ourselves are the most excellent and best sacrifice. This is his City, the mystery of which we celebrate in our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets foretold through oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the Gentiles, from the rising of the sun even to its setting, would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the ways of the city dwellers. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city, and they brought him a good bread. He said, "What is this for, man?" They said, "It is bread to eat." He ate it and found it very pleasant to his taste. **The Rabbi said**: This is made from elevated things. They said: It is wheat. Later, they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And these, what are they made of?" They said: Wheat. Later, they brought him the royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said, "And these sweets, what are they made of?" They said: Wheat. He said: "Surely I am the master of all these, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 1
->1<-
The Priestly Gift <term>Terumah</term> <gloss>the portion of the harvest given to the priest</gloss> and the First Fruits <term>Bikkurim</term>
are alike in that a non-priest who eats them intentionally is liable to death by the hand of Heaven and must pay an added fifth <term>homesh</term> <gloss>a twenty-five percent surcharge on the principal</gloss> if eaten accidentally.
They are forbidden to strangers <note>non-priests/Laypeople</note>,
they are the property of the priest,
they are neutralized in a mixture of one hundred and one parts <note>if one part of the holy food falls into one hundred parts of common food, the whole is permitted to non-priests</note>,
and they require the washing of hands and waiting for the sun to set after ritual immersion.
These rules apply to the Priestly Gift and the First Fruits,
which is not the case with the Tithe <term>Ma’aser</term> <gloss>specifically the Second Tithe eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</gloss>.

## Tractate Bikkurim Chapter 2 Mishnah 2
->2<-
There are rules applying to the Tithe and First Fruits that do not apply to the Priestly Gift:
For the Tithe and First Fruits require being brought to a specific place <note>Jerusalem</note>,
they require a formal declaration <term>viddui</term> <gloss>the confession of tithes or the first fruits declaration</gloss>, and they are forbidden to a person in the first day of mourning <term>onen</term>;
Rabbi Shimon permits an <term>onen</term> to eat them.
They are subject to the law of removal <term>bi'ur</term> <gloss>the requirement to clear all tithes and holy gifts from the home every three years</gloss>.
Rabbi Shimon exempts them from removal.
And any amount of them is forbidden to be eaten in Jerusalem <note>if they become ritually impure</note>,
and their offshoots <note>what grows from their seeds</note> are forbidden to be eaten in Jerusalem,
even to strangers or to cattle.
Rabbi Shimon permits these.
These rules apply to the Tithe and First Fruits,
which is not the case with the Priestly Gift.

### **Torah** is Light <note>Hebrew: <term>Torah Or</term></note>. These commandments mentioned in this Torah portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service <note>Hebrew: <term>Avodah</term></note>, and Acts of Loving-kindness. 

**Torah** consists of the commands "do not add" and "do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers have stated: regarding something that is perfectly complete, it is impossible to say it lacks anything or has anything superfluous. If it lacked something, it would not be complete; if it could receive an addition, it was clearly not finished. Therefore, the definition of the "complete" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is suspended upon His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton</note>, for "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect," as I have elaborated in my work on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah Or." This is also as stated in the Zohar regarding the verse "This is My Name and this is My Memorial": the letters <term>Yod-He</term> with "My Name" <note>Hebrew: <term>Shemi</term></note> equals 365 <note>The number of negative commandments</note>, and the letters <term>Vav-He</term> with "My Memorial" <note>Hebrew: <term>Zichri</term></note> equals 248 <note>The number of positive commandments</note>. It is written, "I am the first and I am the last"; He is the absolute perfection, without subtraction or addition. Regarding this comes the warning, "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," which is a warning against erasing the Name or destroying a stone from the Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are like the House in which He, may He be blessed, dwells; so too is the Sanctuary. It is written, "I am the Lord, that is My Name"; the letters are like the frame of the house and His Name is the soul within them. One who destroys His House, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God."

**Divine Service** <note>Hebrew: <term>Avodah</term></note> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came for there to be a fixed place in the Chosen House, and the Torah gives the reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come." "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the Palace of the Name <term>Yod-Vav-He</term>. Do not fear that she will dwell there, for in the Sanctuary the Glory <note>The Sephirah of <term>Malchut</term></note> is unified with the Beauty <note>The Sephirah of <term>Tiferet</term></note> of His people. This is "to put His Name there," which the Targum renders as "to cause His Presence to dwell." Around the place of holiness, "the wicked walk on every side," referring to the <term>Kelipot</term> <gloss>Husks/Forces of Evil</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see."

### **Sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them within. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn sacrifices from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them, "There you shall offer," meaning there they shall have an elevation <note>A play on the word <term>ta'aleh</term>, which means both "to offer a sacrifice" and "to ascend"</note> and not outside. Since holiness resides in the Chosen House which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn from evil" and destroy all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this hints that the ten nations who do not serve the Lord are idolaters. The matter is that the nations in the Land of Israel, who are under the direct governance of the Honorable Name, serve God through "cutting the shoots" <note>A metaphor for heresy or misdirected worship</note>, and this is true idolatry. However, those outside the Land are under the governance of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of the Sanctuary, so too, conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate the "Subverted City" <note>Hebrew: <term>Ir HaNidachat</term></note> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Similarly, the "Enticer" <note>Hebrew: <term>Mesit</term></note> who misleads others must be uprooted, for he stems from the impurity of the Primordial Serpent who was the first enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the Serpent"; therefore, one does not show mercy to the forces of the <term>Samael</term> <note>An angelic name often associated with the Accuser or Satan</note>. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, as was said regarding the Serpent, "I will put enmity between you and the woman." A false prophet is also like an enticer. 

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the First Fruits <note>Hebrew: <term>Bikkurim</term></note>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. Because the First Fruits are the "Beginning" <note>Hebrew: <term>Reshit</term></note>, they indicate a great holiness, as I have written elsewhere; therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there the priests take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of "Minor Holy" sacrifices <note>Hebrew: <term>Kodashim Kalim</term></note> and the Second Tithe <note>Hebrew: <term>Ma'aser Sheni</term></note> is that they are eaten in Jerusalem. This is the "Grain, Wine, and Oil," which are the primary ancestors of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat Minor Holy sacrifices until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <note>Hebrew: <term>Nefesh</term></note>, and only afterward is it permitted to enjoy the meat. Know that just as the Service—which is the sacrifice—is an offering to the Lord, so too is the worshiper, for the essence of the service is that a person offers himself, following the secret of "When a man <note>Hebrew: <term>Adam</term></note> brings an offering from among you." The Burnt Offering <note>Hebrew: <term>Olah</term></note> is entirely consumed because it comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart <note>The spiritual dimension</note>, and it is offered all night so the Serpent cannot hinder it. Minor Holy sacrifices represent the peace <note>Hebrew: <term>Shlomut</term></note> of the soul and the body.

### **The Secret** of the firstborn is the secret of the "Holy Israelites," who are called "the firstborn of Israel." He has compassion for them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, the firstborn animal is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating sacrifices corresponds to those with blemishes <note>A blemish in a sacrifice renders it unfit for the altar but edible</note>. For Israel is holy and Israel is called "Man" <term>Adam</term>; he was holy at first, but then a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," yet he has a redemption through the secret of "I give a man <term>Adam</term> in your place." This was the secret of the <term>Azazel</term> goat: "And he shall bear their iniquities" <note>Leviticus 16:22</note>. Their iniquities fall upon his head and his people. However, we are commanded not to intentionally cause a blemish in a holy animal in order to eat it, for if one causes a blemish by choice, he harms the sanctity. There is also a prohibition against working or shearing consecrated animals, for even the broken Tablets of the Law remain holy.

### **The General Principle** is that the Service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the Man himself. Likewise, his soul is called to the Altar on High after his death, where Michael is the High Priest. This is a profound secret, for Man was made in the image of God. Therefore, a warning was issued to be careful during one's life regarding the injury of souls—not to kill a person except after the most diligent inquiry and investigation. Only then is it "death by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Lord, may He be blessed, is a True Witness and a True Judge. So too must the Sanhedrin be: just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. By this I mean they must clarify the truth of the testimony with complete clarity, which is inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones."

### **Since** "precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death," because Israel is holy from the perspective of their souls—for after death the souls cleave above—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead, for you are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the other nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, which is appropriate for them since upon death they go to destruction and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. We, however, are children of the Lord. When one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these rituals.

### **Let us return** to the matter: the man who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says, "When a man brings an offering from among you." There is a further secret here: even if a soul has descended to a lower level through the secret of reincarnation <note>Hebrew: <term>Gilgul</term></note>—as in "Man and beast You save, O Lord"—even when eating non-sacred meat <note>Hebrew: <term>Chulin</term></note> for the "desire of meat," we are commanded regarding ritual slaughter <note>Hebrew: <term>Shechitah</term></note>. We must be extremely careful that the blade has no notch, for then the animal becomes a carcass <note>Hebrew: <term>Neveilah</term></note>, and an "abomination is committed in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation may be within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself" implies choosing a "beautiful death" for it—namely, slaughter without a notch. If the animal dies on its own, or if the power of impurity takes hold of it, it is forbidden. But when one slaughters it properly, and if there is a spark of holiness within the animal or a pure bird, then its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats** a limb from a living animal is like one who eats the person's own flesh if there is a reincarnated soul there. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the life <term>Nefesh</term> with the flesh." Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the side of impurity or the side of holiness. I have elaborated on this in Parashat Shemini. When Israel conducts itself with holiness, it is written of them: "They shall make for Me a sanctuary and I will dwell among them," for they themselves are the Tabernacle. Man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart corresponds to the Holy Place; and from the belly downward corresponds to the Courtyard of the Sanctuary, as I elaborated in Parashat Terumah. When one eats foods from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," as I have explained in its place.

### **Regarding** the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals, to ascend for the pilgrimage, and "three times a year all your males shall appear." Do not say that just as he comes to see, he comes to be seen; therefore, if one wishes to appear in the Sanctuary where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Without this, it is forbidden for a wicked person to enter the Hall—how could he wish to appear before the Blessed One and bring a burnt offering of appearance? In such a case, he himself becomes the sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says "three times a year he shall appear"—Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering"...

### Zechariah

And the angel answered and said to me, "These are the four spirits of the heavens, going out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. The one with the black horses is going out to the land of the north; and the white ones went out after them; and the dappled ones went out to the land of the south. And the strong ones went out and sought to go, to walk about the earth; and he said, 'Go, walk about the earth.' And they walked about the earth. Then he cried out to me and spoke to me, saying, 'See, those going out to the land of the north have set my spirit at rest in the land of the north.'"

**And he answered.** "These are four spirits." This is like "to the four spirits." Likewise, "and he came to Jerusalem" is like "to Jerusalem." Another interpretation: "to the son of the black" is like "for the son of the black," and similar cases. This refers to the division of the four chariots, which go out to the four winds <margin>2 Samuel 10</margin> of the heavens. This means giving permission to the four kingdoms to rule in the four directions, each one in its time. This means in the whole world, which is a term for strength. "From standing before the Lord of all the earth." This means as messengers of God who gave them dominion over this. As it is written, "The sons of God came to stand before the Lord." <margin>Job 2</margin>

**Which in it.** "The black ones." He mentions the black ones because the time of the kingdom of Babylon had already passed. The kingdoms of Media and Persia would go out first to the land of the north, for they were there to destroy it, and afterward they ruled over all the kingdoms of the earth. "And the white ones," which refers to the kingdom of Greece, "went out after them" because that kingdom was swift. For Alexander of Macedon <term>Alexandros Maqdon</term> <gloss>Alexander the Great</gloss>, the first king of Greece, killed Darius in Babylon and took the kingdom from him and reigned; and afterward his successors <note>referring to the Diadochi</note> ruled throughout the whole world.

**And the dappled ones went out to the land of the south.** This was the portion of the Romans, for Rome is in the south. Augustus Caesar <term>Augustus Qaisar</term>, who ruled over Rome, began to fight against the kingdom of Greece. At the beginning of his wars, he went out to the land of Egypt, which is the south. At that time, the Greeks ruled in all the lands. Then Augustus Caesar grew strong against them and transferred the kingdom from the Greeks and restored it to the Romans.

**And the strong ones.** These are an allusion to the kingdom of Ishmael <note>the Arab/Islamic conquests</note>, who exerted themselves of their own accord to seek a kingdom, to find a place that would be for them. Therefore, a spirit was given to them. This is what is meant by "And they sought to go, to walk about the earth."

**And he said.** That is to say, he gave them permission to walk about and to conquer lands.

**And he cried out.** That is to say, he called to me with a loud voice and said to me: **"See, those going out to the land of the north have set my spirit at rest in the land of the north."** This refers to the portion of the black horses that went out to Babylon to destroy it.

The person who has undergone evacuation should not rush into consuming many heavy foods, as the nature <note>the innate biological force</note> will attract them while they are undigested. If any such food is necessary, it must be taken little by little and at spaced intervals so it is gradual, ensuring that what enters the body is well-digested. Bloodletting <note>phlebotomy</note> is the specific evacuation for the blood. As for evacuation specific to a humor that is excessive in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is not bloodletting. Every excessive evacuation usually causes vomiting. If the cessation of a habitual diarrhea causes an ailment, the remedy is usually to bring back that evacuation; for example, if the cessation of a nosebleed or nasal discharge causes blockages, its return will remove them. 

Know that leaving a small amount of the matter that needs evacuation is better than exhaustive purging and carrying it out to the point where strength fails. Nature often dissolves that remainder itself. As long as the humor is of the type that should be expelled and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may even need to evacuate until fainting <note>syncope</note> occurs. If a person's strength is robust but the matter of their bad humors is abundant, evacuate them little by little. Similarly, do so if the matter is highly matured <note>concocted</note> or heavily mixed with the blood and cannot be evacuated all at once, as occurs in sciatica, chronic joint pains, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. 

Know that diarrhea draws from above and uproots from below; thus, it follows the accustomed draw and is also suitable after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, drawing them to the opposite side <note>upward</note> or uprooting them from where they are is achieved by the act of drawing and vice versa. The case of bloodletting varies according to the locations from which blood is taken, as you have learned. The people who least need evacuation are those with good digestion, and the inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

### Section Four: Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea and an Indication of the Manner of
### Attracting Purgative and Emetic Medicines

We say: it is recommended for anyone who wishes to take a laxative to take their food sparingly or divided over time, and first determine the amount they will trial in a day in terms of doses. One should use various foods and various drinks; for the stomach, in this state, is inclined to expel what is in it, either upward or downward. As for uniform food <note>non-varied diet</note>, the stomach becomes saturated by it, digests it, and grips it firmly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for those with a naturally soft bowel, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur in those who follow a good regimen <note>health lifestyle</note>; they require what is lighter than that. Sometimes exercise, massage, and cupping are sufficient for them. Then, if the body becomes full, and that fullness consists of the best of humors—namely, blood—then bloodletting is what is needed for purification, rather than purging. If necessity dictates bloodletting or evacuation—for example, in autumn—one should begin with vomiting <note>emesis</note> and then follow it with bloodletting. This is among the recommendations of Hippocrates and the writings of <term>Abila</term> <gloss>likely a corruption of a Greek physician's name, possibly Philagrius or Apollonius</gloss>, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are equal but viscous and cold, bloodletting may increase their thickness and viscosity; in such a case, one must begin with purging. 

In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize bloodletting; if an evacuation is needed after that, proceed. If they are unequal, perform evacuation first until they are balanced, then perform bloodletting. Whoever prioritizes medicine <note>purgatives</note> over bloodletting should have bloodletting performed a few days prior. If someone recently underwent bloodletting and needs evacuation, drinking medicine may stop the effect for him. Often, drinking medicine when bloodletting was actually required results in vomiting and distress. If it does not settle with sedatives, then bloodletting should have preceded it. 

There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that the severity of the illness and the fullness—according to quality and quantity—does not call for. Often, a good regimen makes the bloodletting required at the time unnecessary. Frequently, a reason calls for evacuation, but an obstacle arises; in that case, the only stratagem is fasting, sleep, and correcting the <term>su-i-mizaj</term> <gloss>dyscrasia/distempered temperament</gloss> regarding the fullness. 

Some evacuations are preventative, such as those needed by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in spring. It is necessary to act preventatively before the time and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be bloodletting or purging. Sometimes the external use of drying agents and "blasting" medicines <note>strong desiccants</note> acts as an evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy <note>edema</note>. You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor being evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>a harsh purgative resin</gloss> when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>chebulic or yellow myrobalan</gloss>. 

If a <term>su-i-mizaj</term> <gloss>dyscrasia</gloss> occurs afterward in those with inflammations of the viscera, their purging becomes weak. If forced to do so, use for them things like <term>bindweed</term> and <term>safflower</term>. As for the laxative <term>cassia fistula</term>, it is as Hippocrates said: for one whose constitution is easy, the nature responds to vomiting; the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring. That protects the body from fatigue. Know that one who is accustomed to a slippery bowel or is not used to vomiting should avoid it in summer and beware of it except when necessary. 

One should prepare before purging and vomiting by thinning the humor intended for evacuation and widening the channels at that time, for that protects the body from fatigue. Know that for one who has a slippery bowel or is not used to vomiting, using strong medicine without these preparations of thinning and purging—especially with wasting of the abdominal muscles—is difficult and exhausting. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk during intense hunger, or if the drinker has a slippery bowel, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a purgative may become an emetic due to weakness of the stomach, extreme heaviness, the medicine being repulsive to the patient, or the patient having indigestion. 

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of maturation <note>concoction</note>, will agitate the humor it was meant to purge and spread it through the body, overcoming the body and drawing other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the system. Some humors are quicker to respond to vomiting, like yellow bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, like black bile. Some are in-between, like phlegm; for phlegm, purging is more correct in itself. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with <term>zalq al-am'a</term> <gloss>lientery/slippery intestines</gloss>, the intestines contract and the purgative medicine—especially if composed of medicines with widely differing purging times—becomes difficult. The evacuation then becomes disturbed; the first might purge the second before the second can act, or the first might purge the second itself. 

Whoever is exposed to purging while their body is clean <note>free of excess humors</note> will inevitably suffer from medicine-induced colic and distress, and what is evacuated will be evacuated with great difficulty. In general, when medicine evacuates waste matters, there is no distress; but if it is taken with distress, it is either evacuating something other than waste, or if the humor evacuated changes during vomiting or purging to another humor, it indicates the body has been cleared of the humor intended for evacuation.

### Question 85, Article 3: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, we proceed as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composites are prior for us and simples [are posterior]. But universals are more simple; therefore they are known later for us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the defined comes first in our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later for us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects by chance and at principles [later]. But universals are known later for us. But the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics: that from the general we must descend to the singular.

I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars for us be prior to the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. And what proceeds from potentiality into act first reaches an incomplete act, which is midway between potentiality and act, and then a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a way in potentiality. As is said in the first book of the Physics: things which are more confused are first manifest and certain to us. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. Now it is manifest that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which the parts are contained in potentiality and the integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have cognition of the less common thing: just as knowing "animal" indistinctly is knowing animal in which there is both the rational or irrational, which is to know man or lion. Therefore, it first occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And this reasoning holds if we compare anything more [universal] to the less [universal], just as sense goes from potentiality into act, so does the intellect. And this order

<column-break/>

of cognition appears in the sense. For according to the sense, we judge the more universal first: as when something is perceived from a distance, we perceive it to be a body before we perceive it to be an animal; and further we perceive it to be an animal before perceiving it to be a man, and first a man before Socrates. Or it is pleasing and evident that a child from the beginning first distinguishes man from non-man; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one specifically, as is said in the first book of the Physics. Since things are manifest and someone knows something indistinctly still in potentiality, whether he knows the definition and the principle, thus he knows the genus and is able to know the differences. And so, indistinct cognition is per se intermediate between potentiality and act. And thus the cognition of singulars is prior for us [in sense], but universal cognition [in intellect] follows. If we compare the sense with the intellect, the more universal cognition is prior to the less universal and common cognition.

To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in a double way. In one way, as it is considered through the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth is true and the same holds a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect arrives as the end, and in this way it is truly posterior. As is said in the first book On the Soul: the universal is either nothing or it is posterior. But <note>Plato</note> placed universals as substances; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are nothing except by participation in the more universally subsisting things which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, since in that way things that are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. And in this way the more universal is prior in nature, as appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For "animal" is generated before "man," as is said in the book On the Generation of Animals. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature to potentiality, and the perfect prior to the imperfect. And in this way the less universal is prior in nature, as "man" is to "animal." For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of animal but intends to generate man.

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole; for a whole is that which contains not only "man" and "horse" but also others in the future; not only more universal but also others, like "man" contains not only animal but also rational. Thus, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." If "man" were prior in our cognition to "animal," it would be so through his reasoning.

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing [is prior]. In another way, as they are parts of this whole; and as stones [are parts of a house], it is necessary that we first know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house by a certain confused [vision]. Thus, it must be said that the defining terms considered absolutely are prior to us than the thing defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them. But they are rather the parts.

<summary>Aquinas argues that in human intellectual development, we first grasp general or universal concepts (like "animal") before specific ones (like "man"). He explains that our intellect moves from a confused, potential state of knowledge to a distinct, actual understanding of particulars and their definitions.</summary>

When the Lion woke on the following morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered before him with a record of what Dimna had said in his defenses <note>original: "mu’adhirih"</note>. The Lion took that document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read that document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I am harsh with you, O King, then do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not think you recognize what harms you from what benefits you. I suspect that in your long deliberation regarding Dimna's affair, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand, whether sitting or standing."

Then she stood and left in anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if everyone present is silent and says nothing, their suspicions have united in the belief that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after this accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than confessing your sin, so that you may release your neck from the consequences of the afterlife. This would return a favorable reputation to your name for two reasons: one is your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses <note>original: "al-ma’adhir"</note> to defend yourself, and the other is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: death in what is beautiful is better than life in what is ugly."

Dimna answered him and said: "Judges do not rule based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have learned that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the author of this crime, I know my own self, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only become ugly in your souls, if you are indeed so inclined, because you have suspected that I acted out of malice."

You make the share one hundred and nine parts, and multiply the thirteen by one hundred and nine parts, and add eighty parts to that, resulting in one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband’s share is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister’s portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is that you establish the inheritance shares out of twelve shares, where each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister’s portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy, plus the legacy, equals a sister’s portion. This equals one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The whole estate then equals three-eighths of the estate and three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, and five-eighths of the estate remains, equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The whole estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy, a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is taken only from the third <note>This refers to the Islamic legal restriction where bequests to non-heirs cannot exceed one-third of the total estate without the heirs' consent.</note>.

We have placed the distance from the point of <term>midday</term> <gloss>noon</gloss> because the <term>adjustment</term> <gloss>equation of time</gloss> for the birth <note>referring here to the birth of the new moon or the epoch of a calendar</note> is easier by this method than by calculating from the horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and some fraction. Therefore, the Jewish practice of using <term>temporal hours</term> <gloss>unequal hours that divide daylight and nighttime into twelve parts each</gloss> is not accurate unless the <term>conjunction</term> <gloss>syzygy of the sun and moon</gloss> for the beginning of the month of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> occurs exactly at the <term>autumnal equinox</term>. However, it never occurs exactly then; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have previously demonstrated.

When we extract the time of conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table we analyzed according to their views, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year. We also determine the nature of the year: whether it is <term>deficient</term> <gloss>having 353 or 383 days</gloss>, <term>regular</term> <gloss>having 354 or 384 days</gloss>, or <term>complete</term> <gloss>having 355 or 385 days</gloss>. We already know whether the year is <term>ordinary</term> <gloss>a non-leap year of 12 months</gloss> or <term>embolismic</term> <gloss>a leap year of 13 months</gloss>.

We then look in the Table of Limits for the period of the days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time of conjunction we calculated. We look under the section for embolismic years if it is a leap year, or under the section for ordinary years if it is an ordinary year. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the week for the year and its specific nature. Once we know the start of the year and its nature, and we combine that nature with whether it is ordinary or embolismic, we can determine the arrival of the first day of the following year.

In that way, within the perfectly pure <term>Buddha</term> fields, one is firmly sustained by the joy and bliss of the taste of the Great Dharma <note>the teachings of the Buddha</note>. For example, when a fire is burning in a great wilderness, in some places it spreads, in some places it blazes, and in some places it dies out. the path that serves as the antidote to all obscurations of the <term>perfections</term> <gloss>paramitas</gloss> will arise. The consciousnesses appearing as environments, bodies, and enjoyments are then ceased. Having abandoned the characteristics of the base consciousness, one fully embraces the characteristics of the stainless realm. This very stainless realm is the body of the Buddhas. Once that is attained, the enjoyment body and the emanation body are achieved by relying upon it. This is the established tenet.

According to this tenet, one should meditate on the perfection of wisdom itself for the sake of Buddhahood. Furthermore, this is the wisdom of perfect non-substantiality, distinguished by two types of meaning, because it is certain that the two <note>subject and object</note> do not exist. Those endowed with great compassion are liberated by the six perfections themselves. For this reason, they are addressed as "Great Compassion." Consequently, such a person enters the enlightenment of a <term>Sravaka</term> <gloss>pious listener/disciple</gloss> rather than the enlightenment of a Buddha.

The Bodhisattva endowed with great compassion accomplishes the supreme benefit of sentient beings and directs the intention toward unsurpassed enlightenment, not toward the lower vehicle. This liberation is also achieved by the six perfections together, not by one alone. If liberation occurs through the six together, then what is the role of the first five, and what does the sixth perform?

As for the phrase "Like a lamp in the darkness," it means that just as a lamp makes one clearly perceive a vase or other objects in a dark corner, the co-emergent joy of the example itself makes the bliss that is to be accomplished clear.

To clarify the meaning of the words "I reside in <term>Sukhavati</term> <gloss>The Blissful Realm</gloss>" and so forth, it is said: "The teacher [possessing] the thirty [marks]" and so forth. The primary thing is the enjoyment of the doctrine <note>original: "dharma"</note> together with the <term>bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>awakening beings</gloss> born in that body blazing with the major and minor marks. The "consort" refers to the <term>Vajra</term> Consort <note>the enlightened female principle</note> and the consort of the example. "I reside as the fluid in their <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss>." "Fluid" refers to the seed of primordial wisdom and the seed of the external example. "That" is called the fluid. Therefore, that which depends on the perfect union of the seed, body, and speech is the great bliss. If that is absent, since it cannot arise from any other cause, one must generate bliss from the body of divine union. Consequently, those who seek the bliss to be accomplished must certainly meditate on the <term>deity yoga</term>. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement "One does not correctly perceive external emptiness within internal emptiness," internal emptiness is empty by its own essence. It is not made empty by other forms of emptiness, such as external emptiness. Therefore, the meaning is that one does not seek external emptiness within internal emptiness in order to make it empty. Likewise, one does not seek internal emptiness within external emptiness to make it empty; this is because they are empty by their own essence.

When training in this way, one should understand form, and as it is said, "one should not be conceited about it." This is what it means: just as the clear sky is named in its pure state, so too is this emptiness. In its impure state, it is not distinct from the common person, and therefore it is expressed through terms such as form. However, in its pure state, it is called emptiness. Consequently, the meaning is that there are no phenomena, such as form, that exist separately from emptiness. Thus, because there is no distinction between phenomena <term>dharma</term> <gloss>things or events</gloss> and the nature of phenomena <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>the essential reality of things</gloss>, whenever the nature of phenomena is used to describe phenomena, form itself is called emptiness. Whenever phenomena are used to describe the nature of phenomena, emptiness is called form.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "form itself is emptiness, and emptiness is form," emptiness refers to suchness, the essential nature of form. In this way, because the form that is mentally constructed and the form that is conceptually imagined do not exist at all, and because even the thoroughly established form is not suitable as a basis for grasping, it is said that one should not dwell on form. The same should be applied to feelings and the other aggregates.

"One should not dwell on syllables" means one should not dwell on the individual letters such as A and the others. It is taught that one should not dwell even on that. Because that knowledge of <term>dharani</term> is itself unborn from the very beginning, the letter A is described as the door to all phenomena; through such an expression, realization is achieved. For certain Bodhisattvas with very sharp faculties, relying on this single meaning of non-arising allows it to become a condition for complete and perfect enlightenment. For those with middling faculties, it is achieved by relying on two syllables and becoming familiar with two expressions.

Skillful means consists of the Bodhisattvas accomplishing all necessary goals without contradiction, even though the two systems of <term>samvrti</term> <gloss>relative truth</gloss> and <term>paramartha</term> <gloss>ultimate truth</gloss> appear to be entirely contradictory.

Those purifications of the stages were mentioned previously. This is the purification of the substance of benefiting all sentient beings.

Regarding the statement "complete and perfect awakening, or the dharma to be realized through complete and perfect awakening, is not perceived": this means that through the knowledge of <term>conventional truth</term> <gloss>samvrti-satya</gloss> contained within the <term>wisdom of knowing all aspects</term> <gloss>sarvakarajnata</gloss>, one knows all dharmas in every aspect. However, if one distinguishes them through the <term>wisdom of ultimate truth</term> <gloss>paramartha-jnana</gloss>, then just like objects seen in a dream, one does not see any dharma that performs the knowing or any dharma that is to be known. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement "O Sons of the Gods, because all dharmas are utterly pure": here, "purity" refers to the very absence of any entity. It is a synonym for "utter non-existence."

Regarding the statement "Lord, it is not difficult to manifest complete and perfect awakening to the unexcelled, truly complete enlightenment": this is because all dharmas do not exist. To realize that a non-existent thing is non-existent is not difficult. It is difficult to realize the true, actual nature of dharmas if they were to exist as things. It is not difficult to know and achieve the state where one simply knows non-existence as non-existence. For example, if dharmas did exist, one would have to practice the <term>perfections</term> <gloss>paramitas</gloss> and other conducts in order to increase "white" <note>virtuous</note> dharmas and abandon "black" <note>non-virtuous</note> dharmas. However, because these dharmas do not exist, the practice is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that "it is not difficult to manifest complete and perfect awakening."

The intended meaning behind the Elder Shariputra’s statement that awakening is difficult is as follows: If it were enough to simply remain in silence after realizing that all dharmas have the nature of non-existence and are like space, then it would not be difficult. However, one must realize that in reality there is no such thing as "becoming completely and perfectly enlightened regarding all dharmas," and yet, after that realization, one must still apply oneself to the practices of the perfections and manifest complete enlightenment regarding all dharmas <unclear>one or two words missing or illegible</unclear>.

Regarding the question "What is the knowledge of aspiration?", this refers to any phenomena included within what can be known from the three times and the three realms. This includes all phenomena belonging to the mundane world and those that transcend the world. Because one has made an aspiration prayer to know any such thing, that knowledge which arises immediately after is called knowledge preceded by aspiration, or simply "knowledge from aspiration."

Regarding the question "What are the four total purities?", they are as follows:

1. Total purity of the basis: This is when all tendencies of the afflictive emotions of all sentient beings are completely separated from their basis, and when one attains mastery over taking birth, remaining, and transferring consciousness <note>dying</note> with one's own body exactly as desired.

2. Total purity of the object: This is the mastery over all objects of focus, including those categorized as emanations and transformations.

3. Total purity of the mind: By being free from all negative tendencies of the mind, virtue increases in every way within the mind.

4. Total purity of primordial wisdom: By being free from all negative tendencies associated with the side of ignorance, one attains mastery over an unobstructed knowledge regarding all things that can be known.

Regarding the question "What are the ten masteries?", they are:

1. Mastery over life: This is remaining for as long as one desires.
